nameStory: The silver redhorse gets its name from its silvery flanks that catch the light underwater, paired with the reddish coloration that often appears on its fins and tail. The 'redhorse' part is shared with 24 other species in its group, while 'silver' sets this particular species apart from its more colorful cousins.
description: The silver redhorse is a long-bodied freshwater fish that belongs to the sucker family, known for their downward-facing mouths that they use to vacuum up food from river and lake bottoms. These fish have streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies with silvery sides and can grow quite large, with the world record weighing nearly 15 pounds. They're incredibly long-lived fish that can survive over 40 years, making them some of the oldest freshwater fish you might encounter in New England waters.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy lips positioned on the underside of the head, perfect for sucking food off the bottom - feels rubbery to the touch like a plunger

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, torpedo-shaped body that feels firm and muscular, built for swimming in strong currents

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silvery sides that flash in the light with reddish tinges on the fins, especially the tail fin

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can grow quite large for a sucker, potentially reaching over a foot long and several pounds

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Distinctive forked tail fin with unequal lobes, giving it an asymmetrical appearance

habitat: Silver redhorse prefer larger rivers and lakes throughout New England, especially in the Connecticut River system and tributaries of the Great Lakes. They favor areas with moderate to strong currents over gravel, sand, or rocky bottoms where they can forage for aquatic insects, mollusks, and plant matter.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season brings silver redhorse into shallower waters and tributary streams where they may show more intense reddish coloration on their fins.
seasonality.summer: Active feeding period when they're most likely to be found in deeper pools and runs, often in small schools.
seasonality.fall: Continue active feeding to build energy reserves for winter, may move to deeper water as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Become less active and harder to spot, typically holding in deeper pools with slower metabolism.

funFact: Silver redhorse can live over 40 years, making them potentially older than many of the people trying to catch them - some swimming in New England waters today may have been born before the internet existed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the shorthead redhorse, but silver redhorse have a more distinctly forked tail with unequal lobes and tend to be larger overall. Memory trick: 'Silver' redhorse are the 'senior' species - bigger and longer-lived.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'suckers,' these fish don't actually suck like a vacuum - they use their fleshy lips to scrape and pick up food items from surfaces. The name comes from early observations of their feeding behavior, but it's somewhat misleading about how they actually eat.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative the shorthead redhorse, the silver redhorse grows larger, lives much longer, and has a more pronounced fork in its tail fin. Silver redhorse also tend to have more silvery sides, while shorthead redhorse are often more bronze or golden in coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the silver redhorse, the shorthead redhorse has a distinctly shorter head and snout, giving it a more blunt-faced appearance.
